topics.title: Fundamentals of Nursing
items: Roles and Responsibilities of a Nurse

blocks.text:
1. Introduction to Nursing
Definition of Nursing

Nursing is a professional practice focused on protecting and promoting health, preventing illness, relieving suffering, and advocating for patients and families. It combines scientific knowledge, clinical skills, critical thinking, compassion, and ethical decision-making.

Roles of the Nurse

Caregiver: Provides direct physical, psychological, and emotional care.

Advocate: Protects patient rights and speaks for the patient when needed.

Educator: Teaches patients and families about health, treatment, and self-care.

Communicator: Shares accurate information with patients, families, and health team members.

Manager: Organizes care, delegates tasks appropriately, and coordinates the health team.

Researcher: Uses evidence and may participate in studies to improve care.

Counsellor: Helps patients cope with illness, stress, and lifestyle changes.

Qualities of a Good Nurse

Compassion and empathy

Honesty and integrity

Good communication

Critical thinking and clinical judgment

Responsibility and accountability

Physical and emotional stamina

Respect for patient dignity and confidentiality

2. History of Nursing
Florence Nightingale

Florence Nightingale is known as the founder of modern nursing. During the Crimean War, she improved sanitation, ventilation, clean water, nutrition, and hygiene, which greatly reduced deaths among wounded soldiers.

Nightingale’s Environmental Theory

Her theory states that the environment affects a patient’s recovery. Important environmental factors include:

Fresh air

Pure water

Efficient drainage

Cleanliness

Light

Proper ventilation

Adequate nutrition

Quiet and rest

3. Health, Illness, and Wellness
Health

Health is a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease.

Illness

Illness is a condition in which a person’s normal physical, emotional, or social functioning is altered.

Levels of Prevention

Level	Purpose	Examples
Primary prevention	Prevent disease before it occurs	Immunization, health education, exercise
Secondary prevention	Detect disease early	Screening, regular check-ups, BP check
Tertiary prevention	Reduce complications and restore function	Rehabilitation, physiotherapy, diabetes management
4. Basic Human Needs
Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs

Nurses use Maslow’s theory to prioritize patient problems.

Physiological needs: Oxygen, food, water, sleep, elimination, temperature control.

Safety and security needs: Protection from injury, infection, and fear.

Love and belonging needs: Family support, friendship, emotional connection.

Esteem needs: Respect, dignity, independence, self-worth.

Self-actualization: Personal growth, achieving potential.

In nursing practice, physiological and safety needs usually come first.

5. Nursing Theories
Theorist	Main Idea
Florence Nightingale	Environment influences healing
Virginia Henderson	Nurse helps patient perform 14 basic needs
Hildegard Peplau	Nurse-patient interpersonal relationship
Dorothea Orem	Patient needs help when unable to perform self-care
Sister Callista Roy	Patient adapts to stress and illness
Jean Watson	Caring is central to nursing
Madeleine Leininger	Culture affects health care and nursing care
6. Nursing Process — ADPIE
The nursing process is a systematic, problem-solving method used to provide individualized patient care. It includes assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation.

A — Assessment

Assessment is the first step. The nurse collects information about the patient’s health status.

Types of data:

Subjective data: Information told by the patient, such as “I have a headache.”

Objective data: Information observed or measured by the nurse, such as temperature, pulse, wound size, or lab results.

Methods of data collection:

Interview and health history

Physical examination

Observation

Review of medical records

Laboratory and diagnostic reports

D — Nursing Diagnosis

A nursing diagnosis describes the patient’s response to a health problem.

Format:
Problem + related to + contributing factors + as evidenced by signs and symptoms.

Example:
Acute pain related to surgical incision as evidenced by patient report of pain 8/10 and guarding behavior.

P — Planning

Planning involves setting goals and choosing nursing interventions.

Goals should be SMART:

Specific

Measurable

Achievable

Relevant

Time-bound

Example:
“The patient will report pain reduced from 8/10 to 3/10 within 30 minutes after analgesic administration.”

I — Implementation

Implementation means carrying out the planned nursing interventions.

Types of interventions:

Independent: Nurse can perform without a doctor’s order, such as positioning or patient education.

Dependent: Requires a physician’s order, such as giving prescribed medication.

Collaborative/Interdependent: Performed with other health professionals, such as physiotherapy or diet planning.

E — Evaluation

Evaluation determines whether the patient’s goals were met.

Possible outcomes:

Goal met

Goal partially met

Goal not met

If the goal is not met, reassess the patient and revise the care plan.

7. Vital Signs
Vital signs show the patient’s basic body functions. They include temperature, pulse, respiration, blood pressure, and often oxygen saturation and pain. Vital signs are a major part of health assessment in nursing.

Temperature

Normal adult oral temperature is approximately 36.5–37.5°C.

Routes:

Oral

Axillary

Rectal

Tympanic

Temporal

Common terms:

Febrile: Having fever.

Afebrile: Without fever.

Hypothermia: Low body temperature.

Hyperthermia: High body temperature.

Pulse

Normal adult pulse is 60–100 beats per minute.

Common pulse sites:

Radial — wrist

Carotid — neck

Brachial — elbow

Femoral — groin

Popliteal — behind knee

Dorsalis pedis — top of foot

Terms:

Tachycardia: Pulse above 100/min.

Bradycardia: Pulse below 60/min.

Dysrhythmia: Irregular heartbeat.

Respiration

Normal adult respiratory rate is 12–20 breaths per minute.

Terms:

Tachypnea: Rapid breathing.

Bradypnea: Slow breathing.

Apnea: Absence of breathing.

Dyspnea: Difficulty breathing.

Blood Pressure

Normal adult blood pressure is approximately 120/80 mmHg.

Systolic pressure: Pressure during heart contraction.

Diastolic pressure: Pressure during heart relaxation.

Terms:

Hypertension: High blood pressure.

Hypotension: Low blood pressure.

Korotkoff sounds: Sounds heard while measuring BP with a stethoscope.

Oxygen Saturation

Normal oxygen saturation is usually 95–100%. It is measured using a pulse oximeter.

8. Health Assessment
Health assessment is the systematic collection of patient data to identify health needs and problems. It includes history taking and physical examination.

Four Assessment Techniques

Inspection: Observing the patient visually.

Palpation: Examining by touch.

Percussion: Tapping the body to produce sound.

Auscultation: Listening to body sounds with a stethoscope.

Head-to-Toe Assessment

General appearance and mental status

Vital signs

Head and neck

Eyes, ears, nose, throat

Chest and lungs

Heart and peripheral pulses

Abdomen

Musculoskeletal system

Skin, hair, and nails

Neurological status

9. Infection Prevention and Control
Infection

Infection occurs when microorganisms enter the body, multiply, and cause harm.

Chain of Infection

Infectious agent

Reservoir

Portal of exit

Mode of transmission

Portal of entry

Susceptible host

Breaking any link in this chain helps prevent infection.

Types of Asepsis

Medical asepsis: Clean technique; reduces the number of microorganisms.

Surgical asepsis: Sterile technique; eliminates all microorganisms.

Standard Precautions

Standard precautions are the minimum infection-prevention practices used for all patients in all healthcare settings. They include risk assessment, hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene, patient placement, PPE, and aseptic technique.

Key measures:

Hand hygiene

Gloves, gown, mask, eye protection as needed

Safe handling of sharps

Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette

Proper waste disposal

Cleaning and disinfection of equipment

Hand Hygiene

WHO recommends alcohol-based handrub for 20–30 seconds when hands are not visibly soiled. When hands are visibly dirty, wash with soap and water for 40–60 seconds.

Five moments for hand hygiene:

Before touching a patient

Before a clean or aseptic procedure

After body-fluid exposure risk

After touching a patient

After touching the patient’s surroundings

10. Patient Safety
Safety Measures

Identify the patient before care or medication.

Keep bed in low position with brakes applied.

Use side rails appropriately.

Keep call bell within reach.

Provide adequate lighting.

Keep floor dry and free from clutter.

Use non-slip footwear.

Assess fall risk.

Use restraints only when necessary and according to policy.

Body Mechanics

Body mechanics help prevent injury to both nurse and patient.

Keep back straight.

Bend at the knees, not the waist.

Keep the load close to the body.

Use wide base of support.

Avoid twisting the spine.

Ask for help when moving heavy patients.

11. Hygiene and Comfort
Types of Hygiene

Morning care: Face washing, oral care, grooming.

Evening care: Comfort measures before sleep.

Complete bed bath: Given to patients unable to bathe themselves.

Partial bath: Cleaning only necessary body parts.

Perineal care: Cleaning genital and anal area.

Pressure Ulcer Prevention

Pressure ulcers develop due to prolonged pressure on the skin, especially over bony areas.

Prevention:

Change position every 2 hours.

Keep skin clean and dry.

Use pressure-relieving mattress or cushions.

Provide good nutrition.

Inspect skin daily.

Avoid friction and shearing.

12. Medication Administration
Medication administration requires careful assessment, correct preparation, and safe administration. Nurses must check for contraindications such as difficulty swallowing, NPO status, or inability to sit upright before giving oral medicines.

Rights of Medication Administration

Right patient

Right drug

Right dose

Right route

Right time

Right documentation

Right reason

Right response

Routes of Administration

Route	Example
Oral	Tablets, capsules, syrups
Sublingual	Under the tongue
Buccal	Between cheek and gum
Topical	Creams, ointments
Inhalation	Inhalers, nebulizers
Rectal	Suppositories
Parenteral	Injection routes
Parenteral Routes

ID — Intradermal: Into the skin; used for TB test and allergy testing.

SC — Subcutaneous: Into fatty tissue; used for insulin and heparin.

IM — Intramuscular: Into muscle; used for many vaccines and antibiotics.

IV — Intravenous: Directly into a vein; rapid drug action.

For oral medications, position the patient upright to reduce aspiration risk, and keep them upright for about 30 minutes when possible.

13. Fluid, Electrolyte, and Nutrition Basics
Fluid Balance

Normal adult fluid intake and output should be approximately balanced.

Monitor intake, output, weight, edema, and dehydration signs.

Signs of Dehydration

Dry mouth

Poor skin turgor

Decreased urine output

Weakness

Low blood pressure

Increased pulse

Basic Nutrients

Carbohydrates: Main energy source

Proteins: Tissue repair and growth

Fats: Energy and hormone production

Vitamins: Regulate body processes

Minerals: Body functions and structure

Water: Transport, temperature regulation, and elimination

14. Pain Management
Pain is whatever the patient says it is, occurring whenever the patient says it does.

Types of Pain

Acute pain: Short-term, usually related to injury or surgery.

Chronic pain: Lasts longer than expected healing time, often more than 3 months.

Somatic pain: From skin, muscles, bones.

Visceral pain: From internal organs.

Neuropathic pain: From nerve damage.

Pain Assessment

Use a pain scale:

Numeric rating scale: 0 = no pain, 10 = worst pain.

Wong-Baker FACES scale: Useful for children.

PQRST: Provocation, Quality, Region/Radiation, Severity, Timing.

15. Wound Care
Types of Wound Healing

Primary intention: Clean surgical wound closed with sutures.

Secondary intention: Wound left open to heal by granulation.

Tertiary intention: Delayed closure after infection or contamination is controlled.

Wound Healing Stages

Hemostasis

Inflammation

Proliferation

Maturation/remodeling

Signs of Infection

Redness

Swelling

Warmth

Pain

Pus or drainage

Fever

Foul odor

16. Documentation and Reporting
Documentation is the written or electronic record of patient care. It should include assessments, interventions, patient responses, and follow-up plans.

Rules of Documentation

Write objectively and accurately.

Use approved abbreviations only.

Document immediately after care.

Never erase or use correction fluid.

Sign with name and designation.

Record patient’s own words when relevant.

Document omitted care and the reason.

Common Documentation Formats

SOAP: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.

DAR: Data, Action, Response.

Narrative: Time-sequenced description of care.

17. Ethical and Legal Responsibilities
Ethical Principles

Autonomy: Respect patient’s right to make decisions.

Beneficence: Act in the patient’s best interest.

Non-maleficence: Avoid harm.

Justice: Treat all patients fairly.

Veracity: Tell the truth.

Fidelity: Keep professional commitments.

Confidentiality: Protect patient information.

Legal Responsibilities

Obtain informed consent.

Follow physician orders carefully.

Maintain accurate records.

Report errors and unsafe conditions.

Practice within the nurse’s scope of practice.

Protect patient privacy.
